cards.explanation: The answer is False. Melchizedek does the blessing here, friends, not Abraham. The writer says he met Abraham, forefather of Israel, returning from the slaughter of the kings, "…and blessed him…" (Hebrews 7:1). Keep an eye on which way that blessing goes, because the writer leans on it in verse 7.

The answer is the Son of God. The writer says Melchizedek is "…like the Son of God…" and "…remains a priest for all time." (Hebrews 7:3). Notice he says LIKE, friends. He's pointing at a resemblance, so I'm keeping my words right there with his. I'm just here to stamp cookies, and even I can see that's a big comparison.

The answer is how great Melchizedek was, friends. The writer says "Consider how great Melchizedek was…" and then points out that "Even the patriarch Abraham…" gave him a tenth of the plunder (Hebrews 7:4). That word EVEN is doing the heavy lifting. If Abraham, forefather of Israel, hands over a tenth, this is someone worth paying attention to.

The answer is promises. Melchizedek "…blessed him who had the promises." (Hebrews 7:6). That's Abraham, and the writer wants everyone to notice who is doing the blessing. Think about it, friends: the man who holds the promises still receives a blessing from Melchizedek.

The answer is Abraham, and here's the logic, friends. The writer says "…the lesser is blessed by the greater." (Hebrews 7:7). Melchizedek is the one who blessed Abraham (Hebrews 7:1), so Abraham is the lesser one in that meeting. That's a big statement, since Abraham is the forefather of Israel.

The answer is that he lives on. The writer says "…in the case of Melchizedek, it is affirmed that he lives on." (Hebrews 7:8). Compare that to the Levites, who are "mortal men." The writer sets mortal men on one side and someone who lives on the other, friends.

The answer is True. The text says "…when Melchizedek met Abraham, Levi was still in the loin of his ancestor." (Hebrews 7:10). Levi hadn't even been born yet, friends. The writer uses this to say Levi, in a way, paid the tenth through Abraham (Hebrews 7:9).

The answer is the law. The writer says that on the basis of the Levitical priesthood, "…the people received the law…" (Hebrews 7:11). So the law and the Levitical priesthood are tied together, friends. That's why verse 12 says that when the priesthood changes, the law must change too.

The answer is Judah. The writer says "…our Lord descended from Judah, a tribe as to which Moses said nothing about priests." (Hebrews 7:14). That's the whole point, friends. Priests didn't come from Judah, yet Jesus is a priest in the order of Melchizedek.

The answer is False. The writer says this new priest became a priest "…not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life." (Hebrews 7:16). So it wasn't family line that put him there, friends.

The answer is True. The text says "So the former commandment is set aside because it was weak and useless" (Hebrews 7:18). It's strong language, friends. The next verse adds that "…the law made nothing perfect…" (Hebrews 7:19), and then comes something better.

The answer is that we draw near to God. The writer says the law made nothing perfect, and then "…a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God." (Hebrews 7:19). Drawing near is what that better hope brings, friends. After hearing the law made nothing perfect, that's good news.
The answer is False. The writer says others became priests without an oath, "…but Jesus became a priest with an oath…" (Hebrews 7:21). That's what sets His priesthood apart, friends.

The answer is that Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant. The writer says, "Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant." (Hebrews 7:22). The oath and the guarantee go together, friends. The oath is what God said to Him: "The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind: ‘You are a priest forever.’…" (Hebrews 7:21).

The answer is False. The writer says "…because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood." (Hebrews 7:24). The many other priests were replaced because death prevented them from continuing in office (Hebrews 7:23). Jesus lives forever, friends, so His priesthood stays.

The answer is that He always lives to intercede for them. The writer says Jesus is "…able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them." (Hebrews 7:25). The word ALWAYS matters here, friends. He never has to hand the job off.

The answer is once for all, by offering up Himself. The writer says, "He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself." (Hebrews 7:27). Notice ONCE FOR ALL, friends. The other high priests offered daily sacrifices, first for their own sins and then for the people's. Jesus doesn't need to do that.

The answer is Son. The writer says, "…the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect forever." (Hebrews 7:28). The law appoints as high priests men who are weak. But the oath appointed the Son, friends. That's quite a way to finish a chapter.
